chapter.title: Pike BNF
chapter.p: Caveat lector: This is a simplified grammar for Pike 9.0 and is NOT the normative grammar. The compiler grammar is maintained in src/language.yacc; it takes precedence over this overview.

section.title: Notation
section.p: This chapter uses extended BNF: quoted strings are literal tokens, | separates alternatives, parentheses group expressions, and ?, * and + mean optional, zero or more, and one or more occurrences. These operators apply to the preceding item or group; quoted punctuation has its literal meaning. Whitespace between tokens is omitted.

This is a simplified description of valid syntax, not a grammar for building a parser. Name lookup, constant-expression requirements, valid assignment destinations, type constraints and context restrictions are checked separately. Preprocessor directives are handled before this grammar is applied.

section.title: Definitions
section.p: A program may be empty. Annotations, modifiers and declaration attributes are optional. Annotations precede modifiers; declaration attributes follow them. Class implicit create() arguments are also members, and a variadic (...) argument (if any) must be last and cannot have a default value.

section.title: Statements
section.p: Conditions and loop clauses may declare local variables. The semicolon form of foreach can bind an index, a value, neither or both. The comma-form of foreach requires an assignable destination. Case labels are only valid in switch statements; break and continue targets must be valid enclosing statements.
Note that case ranges accept both .. and ...; the latter is new in Pike 9.0 and is accepted for C2Y syntax compatibility. Type ranges and slicing accept only ...
section.example: block ::= "{" statement* "}" statement ::= init_expression ";" | import | block | ";" | cond | while | do_while | for | foreach | switch | case | "default" ":" | return | break | continue | identifier ":" statement | local_constant | local_function | local_class init_expression ::= expression | type variable_names local_constant ::= "constant" cast_type? constant_names ";" local_function ::= ( "__async__" | "__generator__" )? type identifier "(" arguments ")" block local_class ::= "class" identifier class_tail cond ::= "if" "(" init_expression ")" statement ( "else" statement )? while ::= "while" "(" init_expression ")" statement do_while ::= "do" statement "while" "(" init_expression ")" ";" for ::= "for" "(" init_expression? ";" init_expression? ";" init_expression? ")" statement foreach ::= "foreach" "(" assignment_expression foreach_bindings ")" statement foreach_bindings ::= "," lvalue | ";" lvalue? ";" lvalue? switch ::= "switch" "(" init_expression ")" statement case ::= "case" init_expression ":" | "case" init_expression case_range_operator init_expression? section.title: Expressions and precedence
section.p: The productions below follow operator precedence from lowest to highest. Assignment, the conditional operator and exponentiation associate to the right. Other binary operators associate to the left. The left-hand side of an assignment and operands of increment and decrement must be assignable. Multi-assign, such as [a, b] = values, supports only the = operator.

section.title: Names and types
section.p: A leading dot looks up a module relative to the source file. Scope prefixes select inherited, enclosing, predefined or versioned names. Generic bindings use (<...>). Not every syntactically valid name is meaningful in every scope.

Identifier types include class names and typedefs. Explicit casts must start with a built-in type; a soft cast uses square brackets. Type ranges may be unions of individual integers and open or closed ranges. A bit or bits suffix, as in int(8bit), denotes an unsigned bit width. Array and string types can constrain length as well as element or character type.
section.example: name ::= name_start ( "." member_name )* generic_bindings? name_start ::= identifier | "." ( identifier | string_literal ) | "global" "." identifier | "predef" "::" identifier | version "::" identifier | "continue" "::" "this_function" | "::" identifier | scope_prefix identifier scope_prefix ::= ( identifier | string | "local" | "global" ) "::" ( ( identifier | "local" ) "::" )* version ::= digit+ "." digit+ generic_bindings ::= "(<" ( type ( "," type )* ","? )? ">)" type ::= type_atom ( "|" type_atom )* type_atom ::= builtin_type | name | typeof builtin_type ::= "mixed" | "void" | "auto" | "__unknown__" | "float" | int_type | string_type | object_type | program_type | mapping_type | array_type | multiset_type | function_type | "__attribute__" "(" string "," type ")" | ( "__deprecated__" | "__experimental__" | "__factory__" ) "(" type ")" int_type ::= "int" ( "(" integer_ranges ")" )? integer_ranges ::= integer_range ( "|" integer_range )* integer_range ::= signed_integer | signed_integer? section.title: Lexical elements
section.p: integer_literal, float_literal and string_literal stand for tokens recognized by the lexer. Integers include zero, decimal, hexadecimal, binary and octal literals, and single-quoted character constants. A leading sign is a unary operator, not part of a numeric token. Floating-point literals include exponent notation. Strings support escapes and adjacent string literals concatenate; __func__ also contributes a string segment.

word denotes an ordinary identifier accepted by the lexer, excluding reserved keywords. This includes names containing non-ASCII characters, subject to the lexer's character rules. Operator identifiers and getter/setter names are also identifier tokens. reserved_word stands for a keyword or reserved identifier accepted after an arrow. The abbreviated productions below show their spelling; no whitespace is allowed inside an identifier, a version prefix or a bit-width token. See the Lexical Grammar and Preprocessor chapters for literal and preprocessing details. The current lexical implementation is in src/lexer.h and src/cpp.cmod.
